{{short description|Curve external to a family of curves in geometry}}
{{About||the envelope of an oscillating signal|Envelope (waves)|the abstract concept|Envelope (category theory)}}
[[Image:EnvelopeAnim.gif|upright=1.5|thumb|Construction of the envelope of a family of curves.]]

In [[geometry]], an '''envelope''' of a planar [[family of curves]] is a [[curve]] that is [[tangent]] to each member of the family at some point, and these points of tangency together form the whole envelope. Classically, a point on the envelope can be thought of as the intersection of two "[[infinitesimal]]ly adjacent" curves, meaning the [[Limit (mathematics)|limit]] of intersections of nearby curves. This idea can be [[Universal generalization|generalized]] to an envelope of [[Surface (mathematics)|surfaces]] in space, and so on to higher dimensions.

To have an envelope, it is necessary that the individual members of the family of curves are [[Differentiable manifold|differentiable curve]]s as the concept of tangency does not apply otherwise, and there has to be a [[Smoothness|smooth]] transition proceeding through the members. But these conditions are not sufficient – a given family may fail to have an envelope. A simple example of this is given by a family of concentric circles of expanding radius.

==Envelope of a family of curves==
Let each curve <math>C_t</math> in the family be given as the solution of an equation <math>f_t(x,y)=0</math> (see [[implicit curve]]), where <math>t</math> is a parameter. Write <math>F(t,x,y)=f_t(x,y)</math> and assume <math>F</math> is differentiable.

The envelope of the family <math>C_t</math> is then defined as the set <math>\mathcal{D}</math> of points <math>(x,y)</math> for which, simultaneously, 
:<math>F(t, x, y) = 0~~\mathsf{and}~~{\partial F \over \partial t}(t, x, y) = 0</math>
for some value of <math>t</math>,
where <math>\partial F/\partial t</math> is the [[partial derivative]] of <math>F</math> with respect to <math>t</math>.<ref>{{Citation |first=J. W. |last=Bruce |first2=P. J. |last2=Giblin |title=Curves and Singularities |publisher=Cambridge University Press |year=1984 |ISBN=0-521-42999-4}}</ref>

If <math>t</math> and <math>u</math>, <math>t\neq u</math> are two values of the parameter then the intersection of the curves <math>C_t</math> and <math>C_u</math> is given by 
:<math>F(t, x, y) = F(u, x, y) = 0\,</math>
or, equivalently,
:<math>F(t, x, y) = 0~~\mathsf{and}~~\frac{F(u, x, y)-F(t, x, y)}{u-t} = 0.</math>
Letting <math>u\to t</math> gives the definition above.

An important special case is when <math>F(t,x,y)</math> is a polynomial in <math>t</math>. This includes, by [[clearing denominators]], the case where <math>F(t,x,y)</math> is a [[rational function]] in <math>t</math>. In this case, the definition amounts to <math>t</math> being a double root of <math>F(t,x,y)</math>, so the equation of the envelope can be found by setting the [[discriminant]] of <math>F</math> to <math>0</math> (because the definition demands <math>F=0</math> at some <math>t</math> and first derivative <math>F=0</math> i.e. its value <math>0</math> and it is min/max at that <math>t</math>).

For example, let <math>C_t</math> be the line whose <math>x</math> and <math>y</math> intercepts are <math>t</math> and <math>11-t</math>, this is shown in the animation above. The equation of <math>C_t</math> is
:<math>\frac{x}{t}+\frac{y}{11-t}=1</math>
or, clearing fractions,
:<math>x(11-t)+yt-t(11-t)=t^2+(-x+y-11)t+11x=0.\,</math>
The equation of the envelope is then
:<math>(-x+y-11)^2-44x=(x-y)^2-22(x+y)+121=0.\,</math>

Often when <math>F</math> is not a rational function of the parameter it may be reduced to this case by an appropriate substitution. For example, if the family is given by <math>C_\theta</math> with an equation of the form <math>u(x,y)\cos\theta+v(x,y)\sin\theta=w(x,y)</math>, then putting <math>t=e^{i\theta}</math>
, <math>\cos\theta=(t+1/t)/2</math>, <math>\sin\theta=(t-1/t)/2i</math> changes the equation of the curve to
:<math>u{1 \over 2}\left(t+{1\over t}\right)+v{1 \over 2i}\left(t-{1\over t}\right)=w</math>
or
:<math>(u-iv)t^2-2wt+(u+iv)=0.\,</math>
The equation of the envelope is then given by setting the discriminant to <math>0</math>:
:<math>(u-iv)(u+iv)-w^2=0\,</math>
or 
:<math>u^2+v^2=w^2.\,</math>

===Alternative definitions===

# The envelope <math>E_1</math> is the limit of intersections of nearby curves <math>C_t</math>.
# The envelope <math>E_2</math> is a curve tangent to all of the <math>C_t</math>.
# The envelope <math>E_3</math> is the boundary of the region filled by the curves <math>C_t</math>.

Then <math>E_1 \subseteq \mathcal{D}</math>, <math>E_2 \subseteq \mathcal{D}</math> and <math>E_3 \subseteq \mathcal{D}</math>, where <math>\mathcal{D}</math> is the set of points defined at the beginning of this subsection's parent section.

==Examples==

===Example 1===
These definitions <math>E_1</math>, <math>E_2</math>, and <math>E_3</math> of the envelope may be different sets. Consider for instance the curve <math>y=x^3</math> parametrised by <math>\gamma:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}^2</math> where <math>\gamma(t)=(t,t^3)</math>. The one-parameter family of curves will be given by the tangent lines to <math>\gamma</math>.

First we calculate the discriminant <math>\mathcal D</math>. The generating function is
:<math> F(t,(x,y)) = 3t^2x - y - 2t^3.</math>
Calculating the partial derivative <math>F_t=6t(x-t)</math>. It follows that either <math>x=t</math> or <math>t=0</math>. First assume that <math>x=t</math> and <math>t\neq 0</math>. Substituting into <math>F</math>: <math>F(t,(t,y)) = t^3 - y \, </math>
and so, assuming that <math>t\neq 0</math>, it follows that <math>F=F_t=0</math> if and only if <math>(x,y)=(t,t^3)</math>. Next, assuming that <math>t=0</math> and substituting into <math>F</math> gives <math>F(0,(x,y))=-y</math>.  So, assuming <math>t=0</math>, it follows that <math>F=F_t=0</math> if and only if <math>y=0</math>. Thus the discriminant is the original curve and its tangent line at <math>\gamma(0)</math>:
:<math> \mathcal{D} = \{(x,y) \in \R^2 : y = x^3\} \cup \{(x,y) \in \R^2 : y = 0 \} \ . </math>

Next we calculate <math>E_1</math>. One curve is given by <math>F(t,(x,y))=0</math> and a nearby curve is given by <math>F(t+\varepsilon,(x,y))=0</math> where <math>\varepsilon</math> is some very small number. The intersection point comes from looking at the limit of <math>F(t,(x,y))=F(t+\varepsilon,(x,y))</math> as <math>\varepsilon</math> tends to zero. Notice that <math>F(t,(x,y))=F(t+\varepsilon,(x,y))</math> if and only if
:<math> L := F(t,(x,y)) - F(t+\varepsilon,(x,y)) = 2\varepsilon^3+6\varepsilon t^2+6\varepsilon^2t-(3\varepsilon^2+6\varepsilon t)x = 0. </math>
If <math>t\neq 0</math> then <math>L</math> has only a single factor of <math>\varepsilon</math>. Assuming that <math>t\neq 0</math> then the intersection is given by
:<math>\lim_{\varepsilon \to 0} \frac{1}{\varepsilon} L = 6t(t-x) \ . </math>
Since <math>t\neq 0</math> it follows that <math>x=t</math>. The <math>y</math> value is calculated by knowing that this point must lie on a tangent line to the original curve <math>\gamma</math>: that <math>F(t,(x,y))=0</math>. Substituting and solving gives <math>y=t^3</math>. When <math>t=0</math>, <math>L</math> is divisible by <math>\varepsilon^2</math>. Assuming that <math>t=0</math> then the intersection is given by
:<math>\lim_{\varepsilon \to 0} \frac{1}{\varepsilon^2} L = 3x \ . </math>
It follows that <math>x=0</math>, and knowing that <math>F(t,(x,y))=0</math> gives <math>y=0</math>. It follows that
:<math> E_1 = \{(x,y) \in \R^2 : y = x^3 \} \ . </math>

Next we calculate <math>E_2</math>. The curve itself is the curve that is tangent to all of its own tangent lines. It follows that
:<math> E_2 = \{(x,y) \in \R^2 : y = x^3 \} \ . </math>

Finally we calculate <math>E_3</math>.  Every point in the plane has at least one tangent line to <math>\gamma</math> passing through it, and so region filled by the tangent lines is the whole plane. The boundary <math>E_3</math> is therefore the [[empty set]]. Indeed, consider a point in the plane, say <math>(x_0,y_0)</math>. This point lies on a tangent line [[if and only if]] there exists a <math>t</math> such that
:<math>F(t,(x_0,y_0)) = 3t^2x_0 - y_0 - 2t^3 = 0 \ . </math>
This is a cubic in <math>t</math> and as such has at least one real solution. It follows that at least one tangent line to <math>\gamma</math> must pass through any given point in the plane. If <math>y>x^3</math> and <math>y>0</math> then each point <math>(x,y)</math> has exactly one tangent line to <math>\gamma</math> passing through it. The same is true if <math>y<x^3</math> and <math>y<0</math>. If <math>y<x^3</math> and <math>y>0</math> then each point <math>(x,y)</math> has exactly three distinct tangent lines to <math>\gamma</math> passing through it. The same is true if <math>y>x^3</math> and <math>y<0</math>. If <math>y=x^3</math> and <math>y\neq 0</math> then each point <math>(x,y)</math> has exactly two tangent lines to <math>\gamma</math> passing through it (this corresponds to the cubic having one ordinary root and one repeated root). The same is true if <math>y\neq x^3</math> and <math>y=0</math>. If <math>y=x^3</math> and <math>x=0</math>, i.e., <math>x=y=0</math>, then this point has a single tangent line to <math>\gamma</math> passing through it (this corresponds to the cubic having one real root of multiplicity 3). It follows that
:<math>E_3 = \varnothing. </math>

===Example 2===
[[File:Envelope_string_art.svg|thumb|This plot gives the envelope of the family of lines connecting points (''t'',0), (0,''k'' - ''t''), in which ''k'' takes the value 1.]]
In [[string art]] it is common to cross-connect two lines of equally spaced pins. What curve is formed?

For simplicity, set the pins on the <math>x</math>- and <math>y</math>-axes; a non-[[orthogonal]] layout is a [[Coordinate rotation|rotation]] and [[scaling (geometry)|scaling]] away. A general straight-line thread connects the two points <math>(0,k-t)</math> and <math>(t,0)</math>, where <math>k</math> is an arbitrary scaling constant, and the family of lines is generated by varying the parameter <math>t</math>. From simple geometry, the equation of this straight line is <math>y=-(k-t)x/t+k-t</math>. Rearranging and casting in the form <math>F(x,y,t)=0</math> gives:

{{NumBlk|:|<math>F(x,y,t)=-\frac{kx}{t} - t  + x + k -y = 0\,</math>|{{EquationRef|1}}}}

Now differentiate <math>F(x,y,t)</math> with respect to <math>t</math> and set the result equal to zero, to get

{{NumBlk|:|<math>\frac{\partial F(x,y,t)}{\partial t}= \frac{kx}{t^2} - 1 = 0\,</math>|{{EquationRef|2}}}}

These two equations jointly define the equation of the envelope. From (2) we have:
: <math>t = \sqrt{kx} \,</math>
Substituting this value of <math>t</math> into (1) and simplifying gives an equation for the envelope:

{{NumBlk|:|<math>y=(\sqrt{x}-\sqrt{k})^2\,</math>|{{EquationRef|3}}}}

Or, rearranging into a more elegant form that shows the symmetry between <math>x</math> and <math>y</math>:

{{NumBlk|:|<math>\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y}=\sqrt{k}</math>|{{EquationRef|4}}}}

We can take a rotation of the axes where the <math>b</math> axis is the line <math>y=x</math> oriented northeast and the <math>a</math> axis is the line <math>y=-x</math> oriented southeast. These new axes are related to the original <math>x-y</math> axes by <math>x=(b+a)/\sqrt{2}</math> and <math>y=(b-a)/\sqrt{2}</math> . We obtain, after substitution into (4) and expansion and simplification,

{{NumBlk|:|<math>b = \frac{1}{k\sqrt{2}} a^2 + \frac{k}{2\sqrt{2}},</math>|{{EquationRef|5}}}}

which is apparently the equation for a parabola with axis along <math>a=0</math>, or <math>y=x</math>.

=== Example 3 ===

Let <math>I\subset\mathbb{R}</math> be an open interval and let <math>\gamma:I\to\mathbb{R}^2</math> be a smooth plane curve parametrised by [[arc length]]. Consider the one-parameter family of normal lines to <math>\gamma(I)</math>. A line is normal to <math>\gamma</math> at <math>\gamma(t)</math> if it passes through <math>\gamma(t)</math> and is perpendicular to the [[Differential geometry of curves#Tangent vector|tangent vector]] to <math>\gamma</math> at <math>\gamma(t)</math>. Let <math>\mathbf{T}</math> denote the unit tangent vector to <math>\gamma</math> and let <math>\mathbf{N}</math> denote the unit [[Differential geometry of curves#Normal or curvature vector|normal vector]]. Using a dot to denote the [[dot product]], the generating family for the one-parameter family of normal lines is given by <math>F:I\times\mathbb{R}^2\to\mathbb{R}</math> where
:<math> F(t,{\mathbf x}) = ({\mathbf x} - \gamma(t)) \cdot {\mathbf T}(t) \ . </math>
Clearly <math>(x-y)\cdot\mathbf{T}=0</math> if and only if <math>x-\gamma</math> is perpendicular to <math>\mathbf{T}</math>, or equivalently, if and only if <math>x-\gamma</math> is [[Parallel (geometry)|parallel]] to <math>\mathbf{N}</math>, or equivalently, if and only if <math>x=\gamma+\lambda\mathbf{N}</math> for some λ ∈ '''R'''. It follows that
:<math> L_{t_0} := \{ {\mathbf x} \in \R^2 : F(t_0,{\mathbf x}) = 0 \} </math>
is exactly the normal line to <math>\gamma</math> at <math>\gamma(t_0)</math>. To find the discriminant of <math>F</math> we need to compute its partial derivative with respect to <math>t</math>:
:<math>  \frac{\partial F}{\partial t}(t,{\mathbf x}) = \kappa (t) ({\mathbf x}-\gamma(t))\cdot {\mathbf N}(t) - 1 \ , </math>
where <math>\kappa</math> is the [[Curvature#Curvature of plane curves|plane curve curvature]] of <math>\gamma</math>. It has been seen that <math>F=0</math> if and only if <math>x-\gamma=\lambda\mathbf{N}</math> for some <math>\lambda\in\mathbb{R}</math>. Assuming that <math>F=0</math> gives
:<math> \frac{\partial F}{\partial t} = \lambda \kappa(t) - 1 \ . </math>
Assuming that <math>\kappa\neq 0</math> it follows that <math>\lambda=1/\kappa</math> and so
:<math> \mathcal{D} = \gamma(t) + \frac{1}{\kappa(t)}{\mathbf N}(t) \ . </math>
This is exactly the [[evolute]] of the curve <math>\gamma</math>.

=== Example 4 ===
[[File:Envelope_astroid.svg|thumb|An [[astroid]] as the envelope of the family of lines connecting points (''s'',0), (0,''t'') with ''s''<sup>2</sup>&nbsp;+&nbsp;''t''<sup>2</sup>&nbsp;=&nbsp;1]]
The following example shows that in some cases the envelope of a family of curves may be seen as the topologic boundary of a union of sets, whose boundaries are the curves of the envelope. For <math>s>0</math> and <math>t>0</math> consider the (open) right triangle in a Cartesian plane with vertices <math>(0,0)</math>, <math>(s,0)</math> and <math>(0,t)</math>
:<math>T_{s,t}:=\left\{(x,y)\in\R_+^2:\ \frac{x}{s}+\frac{y}{t}<1\right\}.
</math>
Fix an exponent <math>\alpha>0</math>, and consider the union of all the triangles <math>T_{s,t} </math> subjected to the constraint <math>\textstyle s^\alpha+t^\alpha=1 </math>, that is the open set
:<math>\Delta_\alpha:=\bigcup_ {s^\alpha+t^\alpha=1}  T_{s,t}.</math>
To write a Cartesian representation for <math>\textstyle\Delta_\alpha</math>, start with any <math>\textstyle s>0</math>, <math>\textstyle t>0</math> satisfying <math>\textstyle s^\alpha+t^\alpha=1 </math> and any <math>\textstyle(x,y)\in\R_+^2</math>. The [[Hölder inequality#Notable special cases|Hölder inequality]] in <math>\textstyle\R^2</math> with respect to the conjugated exponents <math>p:=1+\frac{1}{\alpha}</math> and <math>\textstyle q:={1+\alpha}</math> gives:
:<math>x^\frac{\alpha}{\alpha+1}+y^\frac{\alpha}{\alpha+1}\leq \left(\frac{x}{s}+\frac{y}{t}\right)^\frac{\alpha}{\alpha+1}\Big(s^\alpha+t^\alpha\Big)^\frac{1}{\alpha+1}=\left(\frac{x}{s}+\frac{y}{t}\right)^\frac{\alpha}{\alpha+1}</math>,
with equality if and only if <math>\textstyle s:\,t=x^\frac{1}{1+\alpha}:\,y^\frac{1}{1+\alpha}</math>.
In terms of a union of sets the latter inequality reads: the point <math>(x,y)\in\R_+^2</math> belongs to the set <math>\textstyle\Delta_\alpha</math>, that is, it belongs to some <math>\textstyle T_{s,t}</math> with <math>\textstyle s^\alpha+t^\alpha=1</math>, if and only if it satisfies
:<math>x^\frac{\alpha}{\alpha+1}+y^\frac{\alpha}{\alpha+1}<1.</math>
Moreover, the boundary in <math>\R_+^2</math> of the set <math>\textstyle \Delta_\alpha</math> is the envelope of the corresponding family of line segments
:<math>\left\{(x,y)\in\R_+^2:\ \frac{x}{s}+\frac{y}{t}=1\right\}\ ,\qquad s^\alpha+t^\alpha=1</math>
(that is, the hypotenuses of the triangles), and has Cartesian equation
:<math>x^\frac{\alpha}{\alpha+1}+y^\frac{\alpha}{\alpha+1}=1.</math>
Notice that, in particular, the value <math>\alpha=1</math> gives the arc of parabola of the [[#Example_2|Example 2]], and the value <math>\alpha=2</math> (meaning that all hypotenuses are unit length segments) gives the [[astroid]].

===Example 5===
[[File:Envelope cast.svg|thumb|The orbits' envelope of the projectiles (with constant initial speed) is a concave parabola. The initial speed is 10 m/s. We take ''g'' = 10 m/s<sup>2</sup>.]]
We consider the following example of envelope in motion. Suppose at initial height <math>0</math>, one casts a [[Trajectory of a projectile|projectile]] into the air with constant initial velocity <math>v</math> but different elevation angles <math>\theta</math>. Let <math>x</math> be the horizontal axis in the motion surface, and let <math>y</math> denote the vertical axis. Then the motion gives the following differential [[dynamical system]]:
:<math>\frac{d^2 y}{dt^2} = -g,\; \frac{d^2 x}{dt^2} = 0, </math>
which satisfies four [[initial condition]]s:
:<math>\frac{dx}{dt}\bigg|_{t=0} = v \cos \theta,\; \frac{dy}{dt}\bigg|_{t=0} = v \sin \theta,\; x\bigg|_{t=0} = y\bigg|_{t=0} = 0.</math>
Here <math>t</math> denotes motion time, <math>\theta</math> is elevation angle, <math>g</math> denotes [[gravitational acceleration]], and <math>v</math> is the constant initial speed (not [[velocity]]). The solution of the above system can take an [[implicit function|implicit form]]:
:<math>F(x,y,\theta) = x\tan \theta - \frac{gx^2}{2v^2 \cos^2 \theta} - y = 0.</math>
To find its envelope equation, one may compute the desired derivative:
:<math>\frac{\partial F}{\partial \theta} = \frac{x}{\cos^2 \theta} - \frac{gx^2 \tan \theta}{v^2 \cos^2 \theta} = 0.</math>
By eliminating <math>\theta</math>, one may reach the following envelope equation:
:<math>y = \frac{v^2}{2g} - \frac{g}{2v^2}x^2.</math>
Clearly the resulted envelope is also a [[concave function|concave]] [[parabola]].

==Envelope of a family of surfaces==
A '''one-parameter family of surfaces''' in three-dimensional [[Euclidean space]] is given by a set of equations

:<math>F(x,y,z,a)=0</math>

depending on a real parameter <math>a</math>.<ref>{{Citation |first=Luther P. |last=Eisenhart |title=A Treatise on the Differential Geometry of Curves and Surfaces |publisher=Schwarz Press |year=2008 |ISBN=1-4437-3160-9}}</ref> For example, the tangent planes to a surface along a curve in the surface form such a family.

Two surfaces corresponding to different values <math>a</math> and <math>a'</math> intersect in a common curve defined by

:<math> F(x,y,z,a)=0,\,\,{F(x,y,z,a^\prime)-F(x,y,z,a)\over a^\prime -a}=0.</math>

In the limit as <math>a'</math> approaches <math>a</math>, this curve tends to a curve contained in the surface at <math>a</math>

:<math> F(x,y,z,a)=0,\,\,{\partial F\over \partial a}(x,y,z,a)=0.</math>

This curve is called the '''characteristic''' of the family at <math>a</math>. As <math>a</math> varies the locus of these characteristic curves defines a surface called the '''envelope''' of the family of surfaces.

{{quotation|The envelope of a family of surfaces is tangent to each surface in the family along the characteristic curve in that surface.}}

==Generalisations==

The idea of an envelope of a family of smooth submanifolds follows naturally. In general, if we have a family of submanifolds with codimension <math>c</math> then we need to have at least a <math>c</math>-parameter family of such submanifolds. For example: a one-parameter family of curves in three-space (<math>c=2</math>) does not, generically, have an envelope.

==Applications==

=== Ordinary differential equations ===
Envelopes are connected to the study of [[ordinary differential equation]]s (ODEs), and in particular [[singular solution]]s of ODEs.<ref>{{Citation | last1=Forsyth | first1=Andrew Russell | title=Theory of differential equations | publisher=[[Dover Publications]] | location=New York | series=Six volumes bound as three | mr=0123757 | year=1959}}, §§100-106.</ref> Consider, for example, the one-parameter family of tangent lines to the parabola <math>y=x^2</math>. These are given by the generating family <math>F(t,(x,y))=t^2-2tx+y</math>. The zero [[level set]] <math>F(t_0,(x,y))=0</math> gives the equation of the tangent line to the parabola at the point <math>(t_0,t_0^2)</math>. The equation <math>t^2-2tx+y=0</math> can always be solved for <math>y</math> as a function of <math>x</math> and so, consider
:<math> t^2 - 2tx + y(x) = 0. \ </math>
Substituting
:<math> t = \left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)/2 </math>
gives the ODE
:<math> \left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)^2 \!\! - 4x\frac{dy}{dx} + 4y = 0. </math>
Not surprisingly <math>y=2tx-t^2</math> are all solutions to this ODE. However, the envelope of this one-parameter family of lines, which is the parabola <math>y=x^2</math>, is also a solution to this ODE. Another famous example is [[Clairaut's equation]].

=== Partial differential equations ===
Envelopes can be used to construct more complicated solutions of first order [[partial differential equation]]s (PDEs) from simpler ones.<ref>{{Citation | last1=Evans | first1=Lawrence C. |author-link1=Lawrence C. Evans | title=Partial differential equations | publisher=[[American Mathematical Society]] | location=Providence, R.I. | isbn=978-0-8218-0772-9 | year=1998}}.</ref>  Let <math>F(x,u,\nabla u)=0</math> be a first order PDE, where <math>x</math> is a variable with values in an [[open set]] <math>\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^n</math>, <math>u</math> is an unknown real-valued function, <math>\nabla u</math> is the [[gradient]] of <math>u</math>, and <math>F</math> is a continuously differentiable function that is regular in <math>\nabla u</math>.  Suppose that <math>u(x;a)</math> is an <math>m</math>-parameter family of solutions:  that is, for each fixed <math>a\in A\subset\mathbb{R}^m</math>, <math>u(x;a)</math> is a solution of the differential equation.  A new solution of the differential equation can be constructed by first solving (if possible)
:<math>D_a u(x;a) = 0\,</math>
for <math>a=\varphi(x)</math> as a function of <math>x</math>.  The envelope of the family of functions <math>\{u(\cdot,a)\}_{a\in A}</math> is defined by
:<math>v(x) = u(x;\varphi(x)),\quad x\in\Omega,</math>
and also solves the differential equation (provided that it exists as a continuously differentiable function).

Geometrically, the graph of <math>v(x)</math> is everywhere tangent to the graph of some member of the family <math>u(x;a)</math>. Since the differential equation is first order, it only puts a condition on the tangent plane to the graph, so that any function everywhere tangent to a solution must also be a solution. The same idea underlies the solution of a first order equation as an integral of the [[Monge cone]].<ref>{{citation |first=Fritz |last=John |authorlink=Fritz John |title=Partial differential equations |publisher=Springer |edition=4th |year=1991 |isbn=978-0-387-90609-6 |url-access=registration |url=https://archive.org/details/partialdifferent00john_0 }}.</ref>  The Monge cone is a cone field in the <math>\mathbb{R}^{n+1}</math> of the <math>(x,u)</math> variables cut out by the envelope of the tangent spaces to the first order PDE at each point. A solution of the PDE is then an envelope of the cone field.

In [[Riemannian geometry]], if a smooth family of [[geodesic]]s through a point <math>P</math> in a [[Riemannian manifold]] has an envelope, then <math>P</math> has a [[conjugate point]] where any geodesic of the family intersects the envelope. The same is true more generally in the [[calculus of variations]]: if a family of extremals to a functional through a given point <math>P</math> has an envelope, then a point where an extremal intersects the envelope is a conjugate point to <math>P</math>.

=== Caustics ===
[[Image:Circle caustic.png|thumb|Reflective caustic generated from a [[circle]] and parallel rays]]
In [[geometrical optics]], a [[Caustic (optics)|caustic]] is the envelope of a family of [[ray (optics)|light rays]]. In this picture there is an [[circular arc|arc]] of a circle. The light rays (shown in blue) are coming from a source ''at infinity'', and so arrive parallel. When they hit the circular arc the light rays are scattered in different directions according to the [[Specular reflection|law of reflection]]. When a light ray hits the arc at a point the light will be reflected as though it had been reflected by the arc's [[tangent line]] at that point. The reflected light rays give a one-parameter family of lines in the plane. The envelope of these lines is the [[Caustic (optics)|reflective caustic]]. A reflective caustic will generically consist of [[smooth curve|smooth]] points and [[cusp (singularity)|ordinary cusp]] points.

From the point of view of the calculus of variations, [[Fermat's principle]] (in its modern form) implies that light rays are the extremals for the length functional
:<math>L[\gamma] = \int_a^b |\gamma'(t)|\,dt</math>
among smooth curves <math>\gamma</math> on <math>[a,b]</math> with fixed endpoints <math>\gamma(a)</math> and <math>\gamma(b)</math>.  The caustic determined by a given point <math>P</math> (in the image the point is at infinity) is the set of conjugate points to <math>P</math>.<ref>{{Citation | last1=Born | first1=Max | author1-link=Max Born | title=Principle of Optics | publisher=[[Cambridge University Press]] | isbn=978-0-521-64222-4 | date=October 1999 }}, Appendix I: The calculus of variations.</ref>

===Huygens's principle===
Light may pass through anisotropic inhomogeneous media at different rates depending on the direction and starting position of a light ray.  The boundary of the set of points to which light can travel from a given point <math>q</math> after a time <math>t</math> is known as the [[wave front]] after time <math>t</math>, denoted here by <math>\Phi_q(t)</math>.  It consists of precisely the points that can be reached from <math>q</math> in time <math>t</math> by travelling at the speed of light.  [[Huygens–Fresnel principle|Huygens's principle]] asserts that the wave front set <math>\Phi_{q_0}\!(s+t)</math> is the envelope of the family of wave fronts <math>\Phi_q(s)</math> for <math>q\in\Phi_{q_0}(t)</math>. More generally, the point <math>q_0</math> could be replaced by any curve, surface or closed set in space.<ref>{{Citation | last1=Arnold | first1=V. I. | author1-link=Vladimir Arnold | title=Mathematical Methods of Classical Mechanics, 2nd ed. | publisher=[[Springer-Verlag]] | location=Berlin, New York | isbn=978-0-387-96890-2 | year=1997 | url-access=registration | url=https://archive.org/details/mathematicalmeth0000arno }}, §46.</ref>
